title: Bagging & random forests: stronger than the sum of trees
intro: The bias-variance topic ended its diagnosis with a promise: if high variance is the problem, ensembles are the cure. This topic delivers on that promise. Bagging trains dozens of deep trees, each on a different bootstrap sample of the same training data, and averages their predictions — one tree's twitchy precision becomes a stable mean. Random forests add one brilliant ingredient: at every split the tree may only look at a random handful of features, so the trees learn different things instead of reproducing the same tree a hundred times. Including OOB scores, the variance formula that explains everything, and code you run right in your browser.
keyPoints: A deep tree has low bias but high variance. Bagging (bootstrap aggregating) trains B trees on B different bootstrap sets and averages the predictions: same bias, far less variance.

A bootstrap set is n draws with replacement from your n training samples: on average 63.2% unique and 36.8% duplicates — and exactly those unused samples give each tree a free validation set (the OOB score).

Random forests decorrelate the trees: at each split the tree chooses from only m of the p features (m = √p for classification). Ensemble variance is ρσ² + (1−ρ)σ²/B — a smaller correlation ρ lowers the plateau that B trees converge to.

More trees cannot overfit: variance drops monotonically towards the plateau ρσ² and stays there. n_estimators = 100–200 is almost always enough; tune max_features, max_depth and min_samples_leaf instead.
The OOB score evaluates each tree on its own 36.8% unseen samples — a free, nearly k-fold-equivalent estimate without a single extra fit.

sections.title: Why one tree is not enough

blocks.html: A fully grown decision tree is a paradox: unbeatable on its training data, yet its decision structure is flimsy. Swap a handful of training samples and the tree may pick a completely different root split, find different thresholds, output a different leaf — the model snaps at the slightest touch of the data. That is the high variance from Bias-variance tradeoff in the flesh: not a bug but the logical consequence of greedy splits on dense thresholds with no averaging whatsoever. Each tree memorises exactly those details its own training set happens to contain.

The classic fix for a jittery estimator is measure repeatedly and average — which is precisely what an ensemble does. Train a hundred different trees on a hundred different versions of your data, and their individual errors wash out in the mean: one tree agonises over a split another one handles smoothly, and the average stays upright where individual trees whip around. For this trick to work you want trees that are deep and unruly — per-tree bias is low, and the averaging cleans up the variance. The only missing ingredient is a way to squeeze several meaningfully different versions out of a single training set.

One sentence to carry the whole topic: bagging replaces one stubborn learner with a committee of a hundred, each trained slightly differently — and the committee decides. For regression the leaf values are averaged; for classification the trees vote (or the probabilities are averaged first). Everything that follows — bootstrap, OOB, feature subsampling — is technique to make that committee as different, and therefore as strong, as possible.

sections.title: Bootstrap: new data from your own data

blocks.html: You have n training samples and want B different training sets — cloning won't do, because identical sets give identical trees. The bootstrap is the minimum viable machinery: draw a sample n times, with replacement. Every draw goes back on the pile, so the same sample can (and will) be picked repeatedly while some other sample is missed entirely this round. The resulting set always has exactly n rows but a different mix: roughly two thirds of the original samples are present (some twice or thrice), one third is absent. For a tree that splits on thresholds, that is plenty of provocation to learn a different shape.

blocks.label: Probability one sample is NOT in the bootstrap set
blocks.caption: Each draw misses a given sample with probability 1 − 1/n, and there are n draws. For large n that approaches 36.8% — so on average 63.2% of the samples are (at least once) in the set.

blocks.html: Check the number yourself: for n = 100, \( (1 - 0{,}01)^{100} = 0{,}366 \), and simulations with a real random generator give 61 to 66 unique samples per set — averaging uncannily close to that 63.2%. Those 36.8% missing samples per bootstrap set are not waste but a gift: the tree trained on this set has never seen them. Use them as a mini test set for exactly that tree, average those scores over all B trees, and you have a generalisation estimate almost for free — that is the out-of-bag score (OOB), detailed below.

blocks.caption: see the 63.2% with your own eyes
blocks.source:
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 100

for b in range(1, 4):
    idx = rng.integers(0, n, size=n)   # n draws with replacement
    uniek = len(np.unique(idx))
    print(f'bootstrap set {b}: {uniek}% unique samples')

print(f'theory: {(1 - 1/n)**n:.1%} of samples missing on average')

blocks.html: Typical output: three sets with 62–64% unique samples, and the theory line predicting 36.6% missing. The percentage wobbles per set but averages obediently towards the limit — precisely the law of large numbers the whole ensemble idea floats on.

Why draw with replacement instead of just grabbing n/2 samples without it? Because the bootstrap kills two birds with one stone: the set stays the same size as the training data (no information-starved mini-sets), and the multiplicities add extra variety — a sample appearing three times weighs three times as heavily in that particular tree's splits. The replacement also turns the 36.8% out-of-bag fraction into a fixed, predictable fact.

Now the full recipe. Step 1: build B bootstrap sets. Step 2: on each set train a fully grown, unregulated tree (yes — deliberately no max_depth; you want low per-tree bias). Step 3: aggregate. For regression the ensemble prediction is the plain average of the B leaf values; for classification the B trees vote and the majority wins, or — neater — the \( \texttt{predict\_proba} \) probabilities are averaged first and only then rounded. In scikit-learn this entire recipe lives in BaggingClassifier and BaggingRegressor.

blocks.label: Ensemble prediction (regression)
blocks.caption: f_b is the tree trained on bootstrap set b. For classification: vote (hard voting) or average probabilities (soft voting) — soft is usually slightly better.

blocks.html: Why averaging works this well is arithmetic. If each tree errs with mean zero and variance \( \sigma^2 \), and the errors were independent, the variance of the mean would drop to \( \sigma^2 / B \): 100 trees = 100× less noise. It never gets that far — the trees share the same training data, so their errors are correlated (correlation \( \rho \)) and the gain stalls on a plateau. But the direction is right, and that is bagging's power: the bias stays put, the variance drops. Compare with pruning: there you buy variance relief by raising bias. Bagging gets the relief almost for free.

Then the OOB score (out-of-bag). For every training sample, roughly 36.8% of the B trees never saw it in their bootstrap set. Ask exactly those trees for a prediction on that sample, aggregate those, compare with the true label — repeat for all samples and you have an estimate of the test score, without a single extra fit and without touching the test set. It is not full cross-validation (the sub-ensembles overlap), but in practice the OOB score reliably tracks the test score — see the code below.

Practical tip: set oob_score=True on BaggingClassifier/RandomForestClassifier and treat model.oob_score_ as your first sanity check. If OOB is poor while the training score is perfect, the forest is still overfitting (trees too deep, not enough regularisation) — you don't even need a split to see it. For the final verdict you still use the test set and cross-validation (see Cross-validation).

Bagging has one blind spot. The trees differ only through their bootstrap sets — but as soon as one feature is overwhelmingly predictive, nearly every tree picks that feature at the root, at nearly the same threshold, and the trees grow spine to spine: high correlation \( \rho \), hence a high plateau the variance can never sink below. In the breast_cancer data you can watch it happen: worst concave points is such a dominant feature that plain bagging trees look alike. Random forests break that dominance at the only place it hurts: the split itself.

The intervention is tiny: at every split (so at every node, afresh) the algorithm draws a random m of the p features and the tree may only choose among those. Everything else stays as in Decision trees — Gini, greedy, recursive — but the candidate list per node is a sample. For classification the default is \( m = \sqrt{p} \): with 30 features each split looks at about 5 or 6 candidates; for regression it is \( p/3 \). The dominant feature is now simply not offered at most nodes, forcing the trees to discover other structure. Each individual tree gets slightly worse (a little more bias) — but they become fundamentally different, and that is exactly the trade you want.

blocks.label: ENSEMBLE VARIANCE
blocks.caption: σ² is the per-tree variance, ρ the average pairwise correlation between trees, B the number of trees. Derived for the mean of B equally distributed, pairwise correlated estimators.

blocks.html: Read the formula term by term. The second term is the familiar \( \sigma^2/B \): it shrinks with every extra plank of wood, and whatever you do, it goes to zero — at B = 100 it is already negligible. The first term is the plateau: it does not depend on B at all, only on \( \rho \). Conclusion in one breath: more trees always helps, but drowns in the noise if \( \rho \) stays high — and random forests are precisely the knob on \( \rho \). Feature subsampling lowers the correlation, and every reduction pushes the plateau the ensemble converges to straight down. See it yourself in the plot.

blocks.title: The plateau of ensemble variance
blocks.subtitle: Horizontal: the number of trees B; vertical: the variance of the ensemble. The cyan curve follows your sliders for ρ and σ²; green is the dream (ρ = 0: variance shrinks without a floor), magenta the nightmare (ρ = 1: all trees identical — zero benefit). Drag ρ down and watch the plateau sink: exactly what feature subsampling does. The yellow dot is your current ensemble.

blocks.html: At the starting values (\( \rho = 0{,}3 \), \( \sigma^2 = 0{,}8 \), B = 10) the variance sits at 0.296 — already 2.7× calmer than a single tree. Drag B to 100 and almost nothing happens (0.246): the \( \sigma^2/B \) term is all but erased and you are pinned to the plateau \( \rho\sigma^2 = 0{,}24 \). Now drag ρ down to 0.1 and the plateau sinks to 0.08 — an order of magnitude of gain that no number of trees could ever buy. This is why random forests beat plain bagging, and why max_features is the forest's most important hyperparameter.

A persistent myth: “too many trees causes overfitting”. No — more trees cannot hurt generalisation (variance decreases monotonically towards the plateau and stays there). What extra trees do cost is compute, memory and prediction latency. The other way round, the forest can overfit through trees that are too deep and too pure — but that knob is called max_depth/min_samples_leaf, not n_estimators. See the diagnosis framework in Bias-variance tradeoff.

sections.title: Hyperparameters: what to tune (and what to leave alone)

blocks.html: A random forest needs surprisingly little attention — much of its reputation as a “strong default” comes exactly from that. This table is the honest priority list: at the top the knobs that genuinely matter, at the bottom the ones you can leave on default.

rows: number of trees — averages variance out, plateau stays
candidate features per split — THE correlation knob ρ
top priority: try √p, p/3 or log₂ p
brake on individual trees — bias up, even less variance
minimum samples per leaf — gentler brake than depth
turns on the free generalisation estimate
how many CPU cores train in parallel (−1 = all)
always −1 locally, no effect on the model

blocks.html: The tuning order that works in practice: fix oob_score=True and n_estimators=100 first, then scan max_features over a handful of values (√p, half, all of p — the extremes frame the story), and only then reach for the tree brakes if the scores still disappoint. That last step is rarely needed: the combination “deep trees + averaging” is precisely the configuration a forest excels at. If you do want it tighter, use GridSearchCV or RandomizedSearchCV — the pipeline advice from Cross-validation applies unchanged.

Don't forget the scaling step: trees themselves are scale-insensitive (splits look at thresholds, not distances), but as soon as the forest joins a pipeline with other models or preprocessing, you want that pipeline identical for every candidate. And note: what you learn here about max_features and the ρ-plateau logic returns verbatim in gradient boosting and stacked ensembles.

sections.title: Feature importance: what do the trees care about?

blocks.html: One tree you read top to bottom; a hundred trees you read as a story in numbers. The mean decrease in impurity (MDI) — what feature_importances_ returns — tallies, across all trees and all nodes, how much the weighted impurity dropped whenever that feature made the split (using Gini or entropy, see Gini index & entropy). The result is normalised into a distribution that sums to 1: 0.17 means “responsible for 17% of all impurity gain in the forest”. A crude but surprisingly useful look inside the black box.

Take the accompanying grains of salt. MDI is biased towards features with many possible thresholds: a continuous or quasi-unique feature (an ID column, a timestamp) can score artificially high because the tree has so many ways to split on it — the same overfit mechanism as the gain-ratio warning in Gini index & entropy. The more robust alternative is permutation importance: shuffle one feature of the test set and watch how far the score drops — a big drop means an important feature. It works on the test score, has no threshold bias, and warns you when a feature only leans on training. sklearn.inspection.permutation_importance does it in three lines.

Correlation caveat: two features carrying the same signal (say, area and radius of the same tumour) share the importance — neither needs to score dominantly even if the signal is crucial. Conversely a feature may score low while mattering greatly in interaction with another. Use importance as exploration and sanity check (“which group of features carries the story?”), never as proof of causality.

sections.title: In code: from one tree to a forest

blocks.html: The same breast_cancer split as in earlier topics, three models side by side: the unbridled tree, plain bagging and the full random forest — with OOB scores. Note the one-line differences: bagging takes the estimator explicitly, the forest has it all baked in.

blocks.caption: tree vs. bagging vs. random forest (with OOB)
blocks.source:
from sklearn.datasets import load_breast_cancer
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier, BaggingClassifier

X, y = load_breast_cancer(return_X_y=True)
X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.25,
                                          random_state=42)

models = {
    '1 tree':            DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=42),
    'bagging (100)':     BaggingClassifier(DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=42),
                                           n_estimators=100, oob_score=True,
                                           random_state=42),
    'random forest (100)': RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=100,
                                                  oob_score=True,
                                                  random_state=42),
}
for name, m in models.items():
    m.fit(X_tr, y_tr)
    oob = f'{m.oob_score_:.3f}' if hasattr(m, 'oob_score_') else '  —'
    print(f'{name:22s} test-score={m.score(X_te, y_te):.3f}   oob={oob}')

blocks.html: Typical output: the single tree tests 0.951; bagging rises to 0.958 with OOB 0.955; the random forest wins with 0.965 and OOB 0.960. The patterns from this topic confirmed: both ensembles beat the single tree, the forest (with its decorrelating feature sample) beats plain bagging, and the OOB scores track the test scores within half a percentage point — the free sanity check works. None of the gaps is dramatic: breast_cancer is a small, friendly dataset where even one tree comes far; on larger, noisier data the gaps usually widen.

blocks.caption: feature importance of the forest
blocks.source:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.datasets import load_breast_cancer
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier

data = load_breast_cancer()
forest = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=100, random_state=42)
forest.fit(data.data, data.target)

imp = forest.feature_importances_
order = np.argsort(imp)[::-1]
print('top-5 most important features:')
for i in order[:5]:
    print(f'  {data.feature_names[i]:25s} {imp[i]:.3f}')
print(f'  sum over all 30 features: {imp.sum():.1f}')

blocks.html: Typical output: worst concave points leads with 0.172, followed by worst area (0.123), mean concave points (0.090), mean concavity (0.083) and worst radius (0.081); the sum over all 30 features is exactly 1.0. The morphology of the cell nuclei — how jagged, how large — carries the story, matching what the medical literature says. That kind of agreement is feature importance at its best: not proof, but a checkable summary of what the model learned.

Where this leads: random forests are one end of the ensemble spectrum — parallel, variance-hunting, correlation-reducing. The other end is boosting: trees trained one after another, each trying to repair the previous one's errors — a bias hunter. They complement each other perfectly, and together they cover most of the practical tabular-data world. The bias-variance framework from this chapter is the map on which you will keep finding both.
